options: A new kind of engine that rewrites its own deep machinery over time
A standing agent working a maintenance plan, aimed at the system itself
A chat window where you ask the system to fix problems on demand
A separate model trained only to detect bugs in shipped software
the-system-improves-itself.explain: The autopoet is just an agent and a plan pointed inward at the system.

the-system-improves-itself.q: What layer is the autopoet allowed to change?
options: The running engine, but only after a full reboot completes
Any code, as long as the change passes the verify gates first
The declarative layer of plain text: tools, skills, docs, job descriptions
The compiled binaries, since plain text would be too slow to edit
the-system-improves-itself.explain: It edits only the declarative, plain-text layer; the engine is fixed.

the-system-improves-itself.q: How does the autopoet learn what needs fixing?
options: It scans live performance data and forecasts problems on its own
A human reopens the project and assigns it a list of fixes
It reboots agents periodically and watches which ones fail
Working agents file tickets when their own tools fall short
the-system-improves-itself.explain: Working agents notice tool gaps and file tickets the autopoet reads.

the-system-improves-itself.q: Why is 'software that edits itself' safe here?
options: Every change is a reviewable text diff that runs the same gates
The autopoet is trusted, so its changes skip the usual checks
Changes apply only after a human approves each one by hand
The engine quietly reboots to undo anything that goes wrong
the-system-improves-itself.explain: Changes are reviewable, revertible text diffs facing the normal gates.

the-system-improves-itself.q: What is true about the autopoet today?
options: It already reads live performance data and improves with no prompting
Phase 1, the issue backlog, is built and running on this project
It can edit the engine as long as the change is well documented
It is purely a planned idea with nothing actually shipped yet
the-system-improves-itself.explain: Phase 1, the ticket backlog, is real; the self-reading bet is unfinished.

proving-origin.q: Where does a workbook's proof of origin have to live?
options: On a registry server that anyone can query to confirm it
In a separate signature file shipped alongside the workbook
Inside the file itself, surviving a byte-for-byte copy
On the platform the workbook was originally published from
proving-origin.explain: The proof must ride inside the artifact so it survives copying offline.

proving-origin.q: How does the signer's identity work in the seal?
options: It is a name that points at a key stored on a server
It is a certificate fetched from a trusted authority on check
It is a username registered in the platform's account system
The identity string is itself the signer's public verifying key
proving-origin.explain: The identity is the key written out, so nothing needs looking up.

proving-origin.q: Why does verifying a signed workbook ask two questions?
options: To separate whether the seal is genuine from whether bytes changed
To check the signer's name against a master list of trusted authors
To confirm both the timestamp and the network connection are valid
To compare the file against the original copy stored on the server
proving-origin.explain: One question checks the signature, the other checks the bytes unchanged.

proving-origin.q: How is the self-referencing fingerprint problem solved?
options: The seal is stored in a second file so the bytes never move
Fingerprint the page as if the seal weren't there, stripping it first
The fingerprint is recomputed and re-signed until the bytes settle
Only the seal block is fingerprinted, never the rest of the page
proving-origin.explain: Strip any seal, fingerprint what remains, so adding it back can't spoil it.

proving-origin.q: What does a valid seal actually prove?
options: That the workbook's contents are trustworthy and safe to run
That a trusted authority has vouched for the signer's real name
The bytes are untouched since signing, by the holder of this key
That the signing timestamp was witnessed by a neutral clock
proving-origin.explain: It proves continuity under a claimed key, not trustworthiness or true name.

who-sees-what.q: Why is a password box inside a single file not real protection?
options: The password is too short for browsers to check it securely
The file forgets the password whenever it is forwarded by email
The check only works while the original server stays online
The file carries both the lock and the data, readable via view source
who-sees-what.explain: A single file ships the guard with the treasure; you can read past it.

who-sees-what.q: What is the real rule for keeping a secret out of the wrong hands?
options: Keep the secret out of the file entirely, not hidden or encrypted in it
Encrypt the secret strongly enough that no one can decrypt it
Hide the secret in a part of the file most readers won't open
Ask the program to refuse access to the secret on load
who-sees-what.explain: The only way to guard a secret is to keep it out of the file.

who-sees-what.q: Which stance means the shell is public but the data isn't in the file?
options: Public, where everything including the data is baked in openly
Gated data, where contents are fetched from a server that checks first
Gated route, where even the app's existence is hidden entirely
Sealed, where the data ships encrypted but travels with the file
who-sees-what.explain: Gated data means a public shell but contents fetched after a check.

who-sees-what.q: When does the system enforce the stance you declared?
options: When someone opens the file, by running a check on page load
When the recipient tries to read the gated data over the wire
When the workbook is being turned into a file, refusing to build
When the file is uploaded, by stripping the secret before sending
who-sees-what.explain: The guard lives at build time; a leaking file is never created.

who-sees-what.q: What does the seal carried inside a workbook claim?
options: That the file is high quality and safe for the recipient to trust
That the contents are hidden from anyone who lacks the key
That a trusted app store has approved the maker's identity
Who stamped it, and that the file hasn't changed a character since
who-sees-what.explain: The seal proves origin and integrity, not goodness and not secrecy.

secrets-in-the-open.q: Why are hidden sheets and scrambled blobs called theater?
options: The holder owns the file and the program, so any check is skippable
They slow the app down enough that users give up reading the data
Browsers refuse to render files that contain encrypted-looking noise
They only work until the original publishing server goes offline
secrets-in-the-open.explain: The holder owns file and program, so any enforced gate is walked through.

secrets-in-the-open.q: What is actually shipped in a sealed section of the file?
options: The plaintext, guarded by a password the program checks on open
Genuine encrypted gibberish, with the key never riding in the file
A link that fetches the real contents from the runtime each time
A scrambled copy that the app unscrambles using a bundled key
secrets-in-the-open.explain: A sealed section is real ciphertext; the key was never shipped at all.

secrets-in-the-open.q: Where is the key, and how is it obtained?
options: Baked into each copy, unlocked once the user enters a password
Stored in the file's metadata, readable only by the original maker
Held at the runtime; a copy asks the engine, which checks who's asking
Cached in the browser after the first successful unlock of the file
secrets-in-the-open.explain: The key lives at the runtime and is released only after an identity check.

secrets-in-the-open.q: How does the design stop a swapped or relabeled section from opening?
options: It logs every key request so misuse can be traced afterward
It checks the section's name against a list of allowed sections
It hides the section names so attackers can't find the right one
Each key is welded to one section, baked into the cryptographic seal
secrets-in-the-open.explain: The section's identity is baked into the seal, so a mismatch won't open.

secrets-in-the-open.q: What is the 'dead-man switch' property of keeping the key home?
options: Delete the one key and every copy everywhere goes dark at once
A remote command reaches out and erases all distributed copies
Each copy self-destructs after a set number of failed unlocks
The runtime tracks copies and revokes them one device at a time
secrets-in-the-open.explain: All copies fetch the same key, so deleting it darkens every copy instantly.

a-disk-that-travels.q: Where does a workbook keep the things its project remembers?
options: In a cloud bucket rented separately for each workbook's data
On its own disk that rides inside the file and travels with it
On the user's real computer, in a folder the workbook controls
In a data center server that the workbook connects to on open
a-disk-that-travels.explain: The disk rides inside the file; it belongs to the project, not a machine.

a-disk-that-travels.q: What lets the disk answer questions a normal disk can't?
options: It runs a background indexer that crawls folders on every open
It connects to a database server whenever a query is needed
Underneath the paths, the disk is built out of database tables
It keeps a separate README cataloging every file by hand
a-disk-that-travels.explain: Built on tables, the disk answers path access and database queries both.

a-disk-that-travels.q: What happens when you unbundle a workbook's disk?
options: It stays locked in an invented format only workbooks can read
It uploads its files to the cloud and leaves a reference behind
It deletes the originals once the copies are safely extracted
It unpacks into ordinary files in ordinary folders on your computer
a-disk-that-travels.explain: The disk unpacks to plain files; the format never holds them hostage.

a-disk-that-travels.q: Why is an agent working inside a workbook's disk safe?
options: Its writing can reach nothing beyond that one project-sized disk
It runs in read-only mode and cannot change any files at all
A human reviews every file the agent writes before it is saved
Its access to your computer is limited to a small scratch folder
a-disk-that-travels.explain: The disk is its whole world, so even a hijacked agent can't reach beyond.

a-disk-that-travels.q: What is the honest limit of a workbook's disk?
options: It cannot store structured data, only loose unorganized files
It is project-scale, meant for megabytes, not a media warehouse
It evaporates the moment you stop paying for the storage meter
It can only be read on the machine that originally created it
a-disk-that-travels.explain: It's project-scale; big freight belongs behind a bigger machine.

the-disk-grows.q: How does a workbook reach live data outside the file?
options: An agent is handed the password and an open connection directly
An export is pasted into the file by hand whenever data is needed
Certain names are registered to point outside, fetched live on ask
The seal is opened so the file can connect to the outside source
the-disk-grows.explain: Registered names fetch live; unregistered names fall through to the file.

the-disk-grows.q: Where does the password for an outside source actually live?
options: Inside the description file that registers the outside name
In the agent's memory, so it can reauthenticate when needed
Baked into each copy of the workbook that needs the data
With the host, which makes the request through one audited path
the-disk-grows.explain: The host holds the credential; the description only names it, never holds it.

the-disk-grows.q: What is the structurally airtight way to give an agent outside data?
options: A background worker pulls data in and writes it to the disk
The agent reaches out itself but only on a gentle schedule
The agent is granted the password for read-only requests only
The agent queries the source live but caches results locally
the-disk-grows.explain: The worker crosses the bridge; the agent only ever reads a local file.

the-disk-grows.q: Why is meaning-based search cheap enough to leave switched on?
options: It calls an outside model fresh for every query a user runs
Meaning is computed once when content is saved, not at search time
It only searches a small summary instead of the real files
It matches exact letters, which is fast but misses meaning
the-disk-grows.explain: Expensive thinking happens on the rare save; searching is a fast lookup.

the-disk-grows.q: How does a workbook move from a local disk to cloud storage?
options: By migrating the code to a vendor's tools threaded through it
By tearing the seal so the program can name the cloud directly
A few lines of configuration outside the program, not code changes
By rewriting each storage call to point at the new backend
the-disk-grows.explain: The code never names where bytes live; configuration swaps the backend.

under-the-hood.q: What reads the grammar across the whole ecosystem?
options: A separate reader for the browser, the CLI, and the server each
A server reader that every other surface calls over the network
A library that each surface configures to its own needs
A single program, the kernel, a small Rust crate of ~500 lines
under-the-hood.explain: One kernel reads the grammar everywhere, so every surface agrees.

under-the-hood.q: What does it mean that the reading core 'has no hands'?
options: It takes text and returns text; it can't touch files or network
It runs only on the server where the operating system guards it
It needs a human to feed it every file it is asked to read
It delegates all reading to toolkits that hold the real powers
under-the-hood.explain: Text in, text out; touching nothing is why it runs everywhere safely.

under-the-hood.q: Why can the renderer, planner, and safety gate be one machine?
options: They share a server that coordinates the three separate tools
They're the same move: read text, understand structure, answer a question
They each load a different copy of the kernel for their own job
They run in sequence, each one feeding its output to the next
under-the-hood.explain: All four jobs are one machine asked different questions about the text.

under-the-hood.q: Why is the reader deliberately built to do so little?
options: To keep it small enough to fit inside a single browser tab
To make it faster than a reader that can touch the disk
Because hands are where danger lives; powerless code is safe anywhere
Because adding powers would require rewriting it for each surface
under-the-hood.explain: A powerless core can't touch disk or network, so it's safe to put anywhere.

under-the-hood.q: Where do new powers come from if the core stays small?
options: From secretly making the reader bigger over each release
From a server tier that lends capabilities to the reader on demand
From the kernel's six functions growing more abilities over time
From toolkits added on the outside, granted deliberately one at a time
under-the-hood.explain: Toolkits add the hands at the edges; the center stays small and trustworthy.
